questions.question: Which competition win in fall 2012 is described as the more notable success?
options: ICDAR 2011 Chinese character recognition
IJCNN 2011 German traffic signs
ImageNet large-scale visual recognition challenge
MNIST digit classification
questions.answer: ImageNet large-scale visual recognition challenge
questions.explanation: Hinton's group won ImageNet in fall 2012. The first two were Ciresan's niche 2011 wins; MNIST is not a competition mentioned here.

questions.question: Name the four topics listed under 'This chapter covers'.
questions.answer: Understanding ConvNets; data augmentation to mitigate overfitting; using a pretrained ConvNet for feature extraction; fine-tuning a pretrained ConvNet.
questions.explanation: Straight from the box on the page.

questions.question: Why might data augmentation and pretrained models be grouped with ConvNets in this chapter?
questions.answer: Because the chapter focuses on image classification with small datasets, where overfitting is the main problem; augmentation and pretrained features are the main remedies.
questions.explanation: Inference from the bullet list and from p.256, which says the chapter focuses on small training datasets.

questions.question: In what period does the page say computer vision led the initial rise of deep learning?
questions.answer: Between 2011 and 2015.
questions.explanation: First sentence of the introduction.

questions.question: Before reading on, can you say in one sentence what you expect a convolution layer to do differently from a Dense layer?
questions.answer: Self-check: a convolution looks at small local patches with shared weights, rather than connecting every input to every unit.
questions.explanation: Compare with the explanation starting on p.258.

questions.question: According to the authors, when did deep learning finally become dominant in computer vision?
questions.explanation: 2011 and 2012 were the early competition wins (p.255); 2014 was a time of intense skepticism.

questions.question: What test accuracy did the dense MNIST model from chapter 2 reach?
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of section 8.1.

questions.question: In Listing 8.1, what does filters=128 in the second Conv2D control?
options: The size of the convolution window
The number of output channels
The pooling size
The number of classes
questions.answer: The number of output channels
questions.explanation: Window size is kernel_size; pooling is MaxPooling2D's pool_size; classes are the Dense layer's 10 units. p.257 confirms channels are controlled by the first Conv2D argument.

questions.question: Why does the chapter focus on small training datasets?
questions.answer: Because they are the most common use case for anyone who isn't a large tech company.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph introducing ConvNets.

questions.question: What is the role of GlobalAveragePooling2D in Listing 8.1?
questions.answer: It averages each channel of the last feature map over all spatial positions, producing a 256-dimensional vector for the Dense classifier.
questions.explanation: Explanation beyond the page text; the (None, 256) output shape appears on p.257.

questions.question: Why is the input shape (28, 28, 1) rather than (784,) as in chapter 2?
questions.answer: A ConvNet needs the 2-D spatial layout plus a channel axis to apply convolutions over local neighbourhoods.
questions.explanation: p.257 states ConvNets take (height, width, channels) inputs.

questions.question: Can you list, in order, the eight layers (including Input) of Listing 8.1 from memory?
questions.answer: Input, Conv2D(64), MaxPooling2D, Conv2D(128), MaxPooling2D, Conv2D(256), GlobalAveragePooling2D, Dense(10).
questions.explanation: Compare with the listing.

questions.question: What is the output shape of max_pooling2d_1 in Listing 8.2?
questions.explanation: 2x2 pooling of 11x11 gives 5x5 (rounding down). 11x11 is the conv output before pooling, 6x6 would require rounding up, and 3x3x256 is the next conv.

questions.question: Verify the 73,856 parameters of conv2d_1.
questions.explanation: 3x3 kernels over 64 input channels, 128 filters, plus one bias each.

questions.question: Which argument of Conv2D controls the number of channels in its output?
questions.answer: The first argument, filters (64, 128 or 256 here).
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the summary.

questions.question: How can you make a single Keras conv layer use channels-first tensors?
options: Pass data_format to the layer
Reshape the kernel
Set kernel_size to (1, 3, 3)
It is impossible in Keras
questions.answer: Pass data_format to the layer
questions.explanation: The sidebar names data_format per layer, or keras.config.set_image_data_format globally. Kernel reshaping or kernel_size changes are unrelated.

questions.question: If the input were (32, 32, 3) instead of (28, 28, 1), what would conv2d's output shape and parameter count be?
questions.explanation: Valid 3x3 convolution trims 2 per axis; parameters depend on input channels but not on image size.

questions.question: Why does the model's summary show None as the first dimension of every output shape?
questions.answer: It is the batch axis, whose size is not fixed when the model is defined.
questions.explanation: The input shape excludes the batch dimension; Keras adds it as None.

questions.question: Describe the general trend of tensor shapes through this ConvNet and why it is useful.
questions.answer: Height and width shrink while channel count grows: the network trades spatial resolution for more, richer features per location.
questions.explanation: The trend is stated on the page; the interpretation is an explanation beyond it.

questions.question: Can you reproduce the total of 372,234 parameters by computing each layer's count yourself?
questions.explanation: See the math section.

questions.question: What does GlobalAveragePooling2D output when applied to a tensor of shape (3, 3, 256)?
questions.explanation: It averages each of the 256 channels over its 3 × 3 spatial positions, giving one number per channel. (2304,) is what Flatten would give; (9,) would be averaging over channels instead; (3, 3) drops the wrong axis.

questions.question: A model improves from 97.8% to 99.1% test accuracy. Compute the relative reduction in error rate and the number of test errors on 10,000 images before and after.
questions.answer: (2.2 - 0.9) / 2.2 ≈ 59%; about 220 errors before and 90 after.
questions.explanation: Error rates are 1 - accuracy: 2.2% and 0.9%. The relative reduction is the drop divided by the original error. The book rounds it to about 60%.

questions.question: Why is the loss sparse_categorical_crossentropy rather than categorical_crossentropy in listing 8.3?
questions.answer: Because the MNIST labels are integers (0-9), not one-hot vectors.
questions.explanation: The page states: 10-way softmax classification calls for categorical crossentropy, and integer labels call for its sparse version. Both compute the same quantity.

questions.question: Why does listing 8.3 reshape the training images to (60000, 28, 28, 1) instead of (60000, 784) as in the dense model?
questions.answer: Conv2D expects inputs of shape (height, width, channels); keeping the 28 × 28 grid preserves the spatial neighbourhoods that convolution windows exploit, and the trailing 1 is the single grayscale channel.
questions.explanation: The model's Input is (28, 28, 1) (p.256-257). Flattening would destroy the 2D structure that local 3 × 3 windows rely on.

questions.question: According to section 8.1.1, what is the fundamental difference between Dense and convolution layers?
options: Dense layers use ReLU, convolution layers do not
Dense layers learn global patterns over the whole input; convolution layers learn local patterns in small windows
Convolution layers have no trainable weights
Dense layers only work on images
questions.answer: Dense layers learn global patterns over the whole input; convolution layers learn local patterns in small windows
questions.explanation: This is the sentence that opens 8.1.1 (continued on p.259). Both layer types can use ReLU (the Conv2D layers here do), convolution layers have kernels with trainable weights, and Dense layers are not image-specific.

questions.question: What information does GlobalAveragePooling2D discard, and why might that be acceptable at the end of this model?
questions.answer: It discards where in the 3 × 3 grid each feature fired, keeping only its average strength. At this point the map is tiny and each channel already encodes high-level features, so little useful information is lost.
questions.explanation: The authors later (p.265) note that averaging a 22 × 22 map would destroy much more information than averaging a 3 × 3 one, which is why downsampling precedes GAP.

questions.question: Without looking, can you list the four preprocessing/compile choices in listing 8.3 (reshape, dtype/scaling, optimizer, loss) and justify each?
questions.answer: Reshape to (N, 28, 28, 1); cast to float32 and divide by 255; optimizer adam; loss sparse_categorical_crossentropy (plus accuracy metric, 5 epochs, batch 64).
questions.explanation: Check against listing 8.3; each choice is explained in the code notes above.

questions.question: Why does the book say ConvNets are data efficient on images?
options: They have more parameters than dense networks
A pattern learned at one location can be recognized at any other location, so it need not be relearned
They use smaller images
They do not need labels
questions.answer: A pattern learned at one location can be recognized at any other location, so it need not be relearned
questions.explanation: That is translation invariance, and the book ties data efficiency directly to it. The MNIST ConvNet is not defined by having more parameters, image size is unchanged, and training is still supervised.

questions.question: What size were the windows of the convolution layers in the MNIST example?
questions.explanation: Stated on the page; it corresponds to kernel_size=3 in listing 8.1.

questions.question: Describe in your own words how a second convolution layer can detect a pattern larger than 3 × 3 pixels even though its own kernel is 3 × 3.
questions.answer: Its inputs are the first layer's feature maps, where each position already summarizes a 3 × 3 pixel window; a 3 × 3 window over those maps therefore covers a larger region of the image (5 × 5 without pooling, more with pooling) and combines first-layer features such as edges into larger patterns.
questions.explanation: This is the spatial-hierarchy property: second-layer patterns are made of first-layer features.

questions.question: In figure 8.2, what sits at the middle level of the hierarchy?
options: Raw pixels
Elementary lines and textures
Simple objects such as eyes or ears
The label 'cat'
questions.answer: Simple objects such as eyes or ears
questions.explanation: Lines/textures are the lowest learned level, eye/nose/ear the middle, and 'cat' the top. Raw pixels are the input image, not a level of learned modules.

questions.question: The book justifies both properties with a claim about the visual world. What are the two claims, and why does the match between architecture and world matter?
questions.answer: The visual world is fundamentally translation invariant and fundamentally spatially hierarchical. Because ConvNets build in the same structure, they waste no capacity or data learning it, and generalize better from fewer examples.
questions.explanation: Architectural priors that match the data's structure make learning easier; that is the core argument of the page.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why a dense network on MNIST would need to 'learn the pattern anew' if the same stroke appeared at a new position?
questions.answer: Each pixel has its own weight in a Dense unit, so a stroke at a new position activates different weights that were never trained for it.
questions.explanation: If you can phrase it in terms of separate per-pixel weights vs shared filter weights, you have the key idea.

questions.question: What is the shape of each patch extracted by Conv2D(128, (3, 3)) applied to a (13, 13, 64) feature map?
questions.explanation: Patches have shape (window_height, window_width, input_depth); input depth is 64. (3, 3) and (3, 3, 1) ignore the depth; 128 is the output depth, i.e. the size of the vector each patch is mapped to.

questions.question: In the MNIST model, what does output[:, :, 10] of the first conv layer represent, and what is its shape?
questions.answer: The response map of filter 10 over the input, a 26 × 26 grid.
questions.explanation: Each depth dimension is a filter; the rank-2 slice is the 2D spatial map of that filter's response.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does Conv2D(64, (3, 3)) have on a (28, 28, 1) input, and what is its output shape?
questions.explanation: Each of 64 filters has 9 weights and 1 bias. The 3 × 3 window fits 28 − 3 + 1 = 26 positions per axis. Both numbers match the summary on p.257.

questions.question: Why does the book say the output depth 'can be arbitrary', whereas the input depth of an image is fixed?
questions.answer: Input depth is set by the data (3 colors or 1 gray level). Output depth is the number of filters, a hyperparameter you choose when building the layer.
questions.explanation: Output channels stand for learned filters, not colors, so there is no natural number of them.

questions.question: Which pair of arguments are the 'two key parameters' of a convolution in Keras?
options: activation and padding
output depth and window size
strides and dilation
input depth and batch size
questions.answer: output depth and window size
questions.explanation: Conv2D(output_depth, (window_height, window_width)). Activation, padding and strides are optional extras; input depth and batch size are inferred from the data.

questions.question: The bullet says the example 'started with a depth of 32 and ended with a depth of 64'. Check this against listing 8.1. What do you find?
questions.answer: Listing 8.1 uses 64, 128 and 256 filters, so the sentence does not match this edition's model; the general point (output depth is the number of filters and grows deeper in the network) still holds.
questions.explanation: Cross-checking text against code is a good habit; the summary on p.257 shows depths 64, 128, 256.

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 8.3 from memory and explain why the response map is brighter on some parts of the zero than others?
questions.answer: Input zero -> one small filter -> response map; brightness is high where the local stroke matches the filter's pattern (orientation) and low elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The response map quantifies the presence of the filter's pattern at each location.

questions.question: What does 'the same kernel is reused across every patch' imply?
options: The number of parameters grows with image size
The layer's parameter count depends only on window size and input/output depth
Each output channel has a different window size
The output has the same depth as the input
questions.answer: The layer's parameter count depends only on window size and input/output depth
questions.explanation: One kernel of shape (k_h, k_w, C_in, C_out) serves all positions, so image size does not matter. Window size is shared by all filters, and output depth is free.

questions.question: In figure 8.4, what happens between the '3 × 3 input patches' and the 'transformed patches'?
questions.answer: A dot product with the (shared) kernel, turning each 3D patch into a column vector of length output depth.
questions.explanation: The figure labels this step 'Dot product with kernel'.

questions.question: The second MNIST conv layer is Conv2D(128, 3) on a (13, 13, 64) input. What is the kernel shape, the number of parameters, and the output shape (no padding, stride 1)?
questions.explanation: Patches have 576 values, each mapped to 128 outputs, plus one bias per filter. 13 − 3 + 1 = 11. Matches the summary on p.257.

questions.question: Why does the lower-right corner of the output contain information about the lower-right corner of the input?
questions.answer: Because each transformed patch is placed back at the spatial location of the patch it came from, and each patch covers only a local neighbourhood.
questions.explanation: Spatial reassembly preserves layout; locality ensures each output location depends only on nearby input locations.

questions.question: Which two reasons does the book give for output width and height differing from the input?
options: Batch size and number of filters
Border effects and strides
Activation function and bias
Input depth and output depth
questions.answer: Border effects and strides
questions.explanation: Border effects (countered by padding) and strides affect the spatial size. Filters/depth affect only the depth; activation and bias don't change shape; batch size is a separate axis.

questions.question: Write the NumPy slice that extracts the 3 × 3 patch centred on (i, j) from input, and explain how it relates to the book's input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :].
questions.answer: input[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2, :]. The book's expression denotes rows/columns i-1 through i+1 inclusively; Python's exclusive end index requires +2.
questions.explanation: Off-by-one with exclusive slice ends is a common bug when implementing convolution by hand.

questions.question: Can you redraw figure 8.4 and label each stage with the tensor shapes for the first MNIST conv layer?
questions.answer: Input (28, 28, 1) -> patches (3, 3, 1) -> dot product with kernel (3, 3, 1, 64) -> vectors (64,) -> output (26, 26, 64).
questions.explanation: If your labels match these shapes you have the full mechanism.

questions.question: What is the output spatial size of an unpadded 3 × 3 convolution (stride 1) on a 13 × 13 feature map? On a 5 × 5 window applied to 28 × 28?
questions.explanation: n − k + 1: 13 − 3 + 1 = 11 (matches the second MNIST conv on p.257); 28 − 5 + 1 = 24.

questions.question: How many valid 3 × 3 patch locations are there in a 5 × 5 input without padding?
questions.explanation: The window centre must be one of the interior 3 × 3 tiles (figure 8.5). 25 is the count with padding (figure 8.6); 16 would be for a 2 × 2 window; 3 is the output width, not the count.

questions.question: How many rows and columns of padding are needed on each side for a 5 × 5 window to preserve spatial size?
questions.answer: Two on each side.
questions.explanation: The book says two rows; in general (k − 1)/2 = 2 for k = 5.

questions.question: Why does the output shrink by exactly two tiles per dimension with a 3 × 3 window?
questions.answer: A centred 3 × 3 window needs one neighbour on every side, so the first and last row and column cannot be centres: one tile is lost at each end of each axis.
questions.explanation: This is the border effect the page describes; padding supplies the missing neighbours.

questions.question: In figure 8.6, what do the tiles drawn with crosses represent?
options: Pixels that are masked by dropout
Padding added around the 5 × 5 input
Tiles with zero activation in the output
Positions skipped by a stride
questions.answer: Padding added around the 5 × 5 input
questions.explanation: The figure shows the 5 × 5 input surrounded by a ring of padding tiles, giving a 7 × 7 grid from which 25 patches can be extracted. Dropout and strides are unrelated; the crossed tiles are on the input side.

questions.question: Using the shapes in the MNIST model summary, identify every place the border effect occurs and every place something else changes the size.
questions.answer: Border effect: 28→26, 13→11, 5→3 (each Conv2D). Max pooling: 26→13, 11→5 (halving with flooring).
questions.explanation: Each unpadded 3 × 3 conv loses 2; pooling (p.263) halves.

questions.question: Can you draw a 4 × 4 input and mark the valid centres of a 3 × 3 window, then say what padding would make the output 4 × 4?
questions.answer: Valid centres are the 2 × 2 interior tiles (output 2 × 2); padding one row/column on each side gives a 6 × 6 grid and a 4 × 4 output.
questions.explanation: Apply n − k + 1 and p = (k − 1)/2.

questions.question: What is the default value of Conv2D's padding argument?
options: "same"
"valid"
"causal"
"full"
questions.answer: "valid"
questions.explanation: The page states the default is "valid" (no padding). "same" must be requested explicitly; "causal" and "full" are not the Conv2D default.

questions.question: A 3 × 3 convolution with stride 2 and no padding is applied to a 5 × 5 input (figure 8.7). How many patches are extracted and what is the output size? What about a 7 × 7 input?
questions.answer: 4 patches, 2 × 2 output; for 7 × 7: ⌊(7 − 3)/2⌋ + 1 = 3, a 3 × 3 output (9 patches).
questions.explanation: Valid centres are the interior tiles; stride 2 keeps every other one.

questions.question: What is a stride?
questions.answer: The distance between two successive convolution windows; it defaults to 1.
questions.explanation: Defined in the 'Understanding convolution strides' paragraph.

questions.question: What does the book mean by 'downsampled by a factor of 2 (in addition to any changes induced by border effects)'? Give the output size of a 3 × 3 stride-2 convolution on 28 × 28 with "valid" and with "same" padding.
questions.answer: Stride halves the size, and valid padding additionally loses border tiles: "valid" gives 13 × 13, "same" gives 14 × 14.

questions.question: According to the page, which operation do classification models tend to use to downsample feature maps?
options: Strided convolutions
Max pooling
Padding
Global average pooling at every layer
questions.answer: Max pooling
questions.explanation: The book says strided convolutions are rarely used in classification models; instead max pooling is used. Padding doesn't downsample, and global average pooling is used once at the end (p.258).

questions.question: In the MNIST ConvNet, the second MaxPooling2D receives an 11 × 11 map. What does it output, and why not 5.5 × 5.5 or 6 × 6?
questions.answer: 5 × 5: with 2 × 2 windows and stride 2 only 5 full windows fit along each axis; the last row/column is dropped.
questions.explanation: Pooling uses valid windows by default, so the size is floored (⌊11/2⌋ = 5), as shown in the summary on p.257.

questions.question: Can you explain, for each layer of the MNIST model, which of the three effects (border effect, stride, pooling) changes its spatial size?
questions.answer: Conv layers: border effect only (valid padding, stride 1): −2. Pooling layers: halving. Strides are not used.
questions.explanation: If you can produce 28→26→13→11→5→3 from these rules, you've mastered pages 262-263.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the key difference between how convolution and max pooling transform local patches?
options: Convolution uses a learned linear transformation; max pooling uses a hardcoded max operation
Convolution works per channel; max pooling mixes all channels
Max pooling uses 3 × 3 windows; convolution uses 2 × 2 windows
Max pooling has more trainable parameters than convolution
questions.answer: Convolution uses a learned linear transformation; max pooling uses a hardcoded max operation
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this. The second option is reversed: convolution mixes channels and pooling is per channel. The window sizes are swapped in the third option. Pooling has zero parameters.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count 73,856 for conv2d_4 in the summary.
questions.explanation: Each of the 128 filters has a 3 × 3 × 64 kernel (64 input channels from the previous layer) plus one bias.

questions.question: Why does the spatial size go 28 → 26 → 24 → 22 in Listing 8.5?
questions.answer: Each 3 × 3 convolution uses valid padding (the default) and stride 1, so it loses one pixel on each border: output = input − 3 + 1.
questions.explanation: There is no pooling or stride, so the border effect described on p.262-263 is the only source of shrinkage.

questions.question: Explain why the third layer's 3 × 3 windows correspond to 7 × 7 windows in the input, and why that is a problem for classifying digits.
questions.answer: Each stride-1 3 × 3 layer expands the region of input seen by 2 pixels (3 → 5 → 7). A 7 × 7 patch is a small fraction of a 28 × 28 digit, so even the last layer's features are local and cannot encode the digit's global shape.
questions.explanation: The book makes this point as the first of two problems (continued on p.265). Downsampling lets receptive fields grow much faster.

questions.question: A feature map of shape (26, 26, 64) passes through MaxPooling2D with 2 × 2 windows and stride 2. What is the output shape?
questions.explanation: Height and width are halved; max pooling works per channel, so the channel count stays 64. (13, 13, 32) wrongly halves channels, (24, 24, 64) is what a 3 × 3 valid convolution would give, and (26, 26, 16) confuses pooling with channel reduction.

questions.question: Removing the max-pooling layers did not cause a parameter explosion here (372,234 parameters). So what is the real cost of omitting them?
questions.answer: The cost is architectural and computational. Receptive fields stay tiny (no spatial hierarchy), the final feature map is large (22 × 22), so global averaging throws away a lot of information, and every late layer computes over many more positions.
questions.explanation: Conv parameters don't depend on spatial size. The two problems named by the book (p.264-265) are about hierarchy and the information carried by the final map.

questions.question: Without looking, can you compute every row of the summary table (shape and Param #) from Listing 8.5 alone?
questions.explanation: If you can, you understand valid convolutions, weight sharing and global pooling.

questions.question: What are the two problems with the pooling-free ConvNet of Listing 8.5?
questions.answer: (1) It doesn't learn a spatial hierarchy: third-layer features only see 7 × 7 input windows. (2) The final 22 × 22 feature map is huge, so global averaging destroys a lot of information.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the bullets spanning p.264-265.

questions.question: Why, according to the authors, does max pooling tend to work better than average pooling?
options: Features encode the spatial presence of patterns, and maximal presence is more informative than average presence
Max pooling has learnable weights that adapt to the data
Average pooling cannot reduce spatial resolution
Max pooling increases the number of channels
questions.answer: Features encode the spatial presence of patterns, and maximal presence is more informative than average presence
questions.explanation: This is the stated reason. Max pooling has no weights, average pooling also downsamples, and neither changes the channel count.

questions.question: Why is 'dense unstrided convolutions followed by max pooling' preferred to 'strided convolutions' for downsampling in classification?
questions.answer: Unstrided convolutions evaluate every location, producing dense feature maps. Max pooling then keeps the strongest response in each patch. Strided convolutions look at sparser windows and can miss feature presence.
questions.explanation: The page says sparser windows or averaging "could cause you to miss or dilute feature-presence information." The trade-off flips when exact location matters (p.339).

questions.question: How is the 5,000-image cats-vs-dogs subset split in section 8.2?
options: 2,000 train / 1,000 validation / 2,000 test
4,000 train / 500 validation / 500 test
2,500 train / 2,500 test
3,000 train / 1,000 validation / 1,000 test
questions.answer: 2,000 train / 1,000 validation / 2,000 test
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page. The 2,500/2,500 figure is the per-class count (cats/dogs), not a split.

questions.question: A 2 × 2 window of one channel contains [0, 0, 0, 8]. What do max and average pooling output, and what does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Max = 8, average = 2. Averaging dilutes a single strong feature detection by a factor of 4.
questions.explanation: This illustrates the book's 'maximal presence vs. average presence' argument.

questions.question: What does it mean that downsampling makes information 'less spatially distributed and increasingly contained in the channels'?
questions.answer: As height and width shrink while the number of filters grows, each spatial position summarizes a larger region, and what is present is encoded by which channels are active rather than by where activations occur.
questions.explanation: This paraphrases the 'In short' paragraph. It is the reason for the pyramid shape of ConvNets (p.269).

questions.question: Can you predict the accuracy milestones of chapter 8's strategies and name the main issue of the naive baseline?
questions.answer: From scratch ≈80%, with augmentation ≈84%, pretrained fine-tuning 98.5%. The main issue of the baseline is overfitting.
questions.explanation: Stated on p.265-266.

questions.question: Which property does the page give for why ConvNets are highly data efficient on perceptual problems?
options: They learn local, translation-invariant features
They have more parameters than dense networks
They require custom feature engineering
They use max pooling instead of strides
questions.answer: They learn local, translation-invariant features
questions.explanation: Stated directly in 8.2.1. ConvNets usually have fewer parameters, the page says no feature engineering is needed, and the pooling choice is not the stated reason.

questions.question: What are the three strategies in the 'toolbox', and what accuracies does the chapter report for the milestones?
questions.answer: Training a small model from scratch (≈80%, ≈84% with data augmentation), feature extraction with a pretrained model, and fine-tuning a pretrained model (98.5% final).
questions.explanation: Listed across p.265-266.

questions.question: Why does the book say that what qualifies as 'enough samples' is relative?
questions.answer: It depends on the size and depth of the model, on regularization and on the complexity of the task. A few hundred samples can be enough for a small, well-regularized model on a simple task, but a few tens are not enough for a complex problem.
questions.explanation: Data requirements scale with how many hypotheses the model can represent and with how hard the target function is.

questions.question: What problem is data augmentation introduced to address?
options: Overfitting
Vanishing gradients
Class imbalance
Slow GPU training
questions.answer: Overfitting
questions.explanation: The page says the main issue will be overfitting and introduces augmentation as a technique for mitigating it. The classes are balanced (2,500 each), and gradients and speed are not discussed.

questions.question: What does 'feature reuse' mean, and why does it matter for small datasets?
questions.answer: Representations learned by a model trained on a large dataset can be reused for a different problem with minor changes. A small dataset then only needs to teach the task-specific part.
questions.explanation: The book calls this one of the greatest strengths of deep learning; section 8.3 applies it.

questions.question: Can you set up the Dogs vs. Cats download in Colab with kagglehub (account, competition rules, API key)?
questions.answer: Join the competition at kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/rules, generate an API key in settings, log in with kagglehub, download, then unzip train.zip (p.267).
questions.explanation: The sidebar starts here and lists the steps on p.267.

questions.question: What two things must you do on the Kaggle website before downloading the data from code?
questions.answer: Join the competition (accept the rules) at kaggle.com/c/dogs-vs-cats/rules, and generate an API key at kaggle.com/settings.
questions.explanation: These are steps 1 and 2 at the top of the page.

questions.question: Which files does kagglehub.competition_download("dogs-vs-cats") produce?
options: train.zip and test1.zip
train/ and validation/ folders
A single cats_vs_dogs.npz file
A TFRecord dataset
questions.answer: train.zip and test1.zip
questions.explanation: The page says it downloads train.zip and test1.zip. The split folders are created later by the authors (p.268), and no npz or TFRecord file is involved.

questions.question: Why does the chapter only use train.zip?
questions.answer: It contains the labelled images. The authors build their own training, validation and test subsets from it (p.268). The competition test images are not needed.
questions.explanation: The book says 'We'll only use the training data here'. The note that the competition test set is unlabeled is an explanation beyond the book.

questions.question: What does figure 8.8 tell you about the preprocessing that will be required?
questions.answer: The images differ in size, colour and background, so they must be decoded and resized to a common shape (180 × 180 on p.269) before they can be batched as tensors.
questions.explanation: Neural networks need fixed-shape inputs within a batch.

questions.question: What does `zip_ref.extractall(".")` do?
options: Extracts all files from the archive into the current directory
Extracts only image files into a new temp directory
Deletes the zip after reading it
Loads the images into memory as a NumPy array
questions.answer: Extracts all files from the archive into the current directory
questions.explanation: '.' is the current working directory, and extractall extracts every member. It doesn't filter files, delete the archive or load arrays.

questions.question: Have you run these three snippets and checked that a train/ folder with about 25,000 JPEGs exists?
questions.answer: You should see files like cat.0.jpg … dog.12499.jpg (the file naming is used on p.268).
questions.explanation: The next listing depends on this directory being present.

questions.question: How many cat images does dogs_vs_cats_small/validation/cat contain?
questions.explanation: The validation set has 500 samples of each class. 1,000 is the per-class count for train and test, and 12,500 is the per-class total of the full dataset.

questions.question: What fraction of the original data is used for training, and why do the authors use so little?
questions.answer: 2,000 of 25,000 images (8%, 'less than 10%'). Many real image datasets only have a few thousand samples, so it's good practice to learn with a small dataset.
questions.explanation: Both facts are on the page.

questions.question: Why is the class-per-subfolder layout (train/cat, train/dog, …) convenient?
questions.answer: The label of every image is implied by its folder, so a loading utility can infer labels from directory names without a separate label file.
questions.explanation: This is an inference about the next steps (directory-based loading on p.271); the page itself only shows the structure.

questions.question: In Listing 8.6, what does `new_base_dir / subset_name / category` produce?
options: A pathlib.Path such as dogs_vs_cats_small/train/cat
A floating-point division result
A list of file names
A string containing only the category name
questions.answer: A pathlib.Path such as dogs_vs_cats_small/train/cat
questions.explanation: pathlib overloads / to join path components. It is not arithmetic, and the file list is built separately on p.269.

questions.question: What happens if you run Listing 8.6 twice, and how could you fix it?
questions.answer: os.makedirs raises FileExistsError because the directories already exist. Delete the folder first or pass exist_ok=True.
questions.explanation: This is standard os.makedirs behaviour (an explanation beyond the book).

questions.question: Can you state the 2013 competition's best accuracy and the full dataset's size and class balance without looking?
questions.answer: Up to 95%; 25,000 images, 12,500 per class, 543 MB compressed.
questions.explanation: These are the reference numbers for judging the chapter's results.

questions.question: Which indices of each category go into the validation subset?
options: 1000 to 1500 inclusive
questions.explanation: make_subset("validation", start_index=1000, end_index=1500) uses range(1000, 1500), which excludes 1500. 0-999 is train, 1500-2499 is test, and 'inclusive' would give 501 images.

questions.question: Why do the authors say accuracy is an appropriate measure of success here?
questions.answer: Each split has the same number of cats and dogs (balanced binary classification), so accuracy isn't inflated by a majority class; chance level is 50%.
questions.explanation: With imbalanced classes, a model that always predicts the majority class could score high accuracy.

questions.question: What two purposes do the two extra Conv2D/MaxPooling2D stages serve?
questions.answer: They increase the model's capacity and further reduce the feature-map size so the maps aren't overly large at the global pooling layer (ending at 7 × 7).
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of 8.2.3. This connects to the second defect of Listing 8.5 (p.265).

questions.question: What output layer does the model use, and why?
options: Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"), because it is a binary classification problem
Dense(2, activation="relu"), because there are two classes
Dense(10, activation="softmax"), as in MNIST
No Dense layer; GlobalAveragePooling2D outputs the probability directly
questions.answer: Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"), because it is a binary classification problem
questions.explanation: One sigmoid unit encodes the probability of one class versus the other. ReLU outputs are not probabilities, 10 classes is MNIST, and global pooling outputs a 512-vector, not a probability.

questions.question: Starting from 180 × 180, apply 'valid 3×3 conv then 2×2 max pool' four times, then one more valid 3×3 conv. What final spatial size do you get?
questions.explanation: This matches the 7 × 7 the book reports just before GlobalAveragePooling2D. The exact layer list appears on p.270.

questions.question: What is the 'depth up, size down' pattern, and how does it relate to the max-pooling discussion on p.265?
questions.answer: The number of channels increases (32 → 512) as spatial size decreases (180 → 7). Downsampling moves information from spatial positions into channels, so more channels are needed to hold richer, more abstract features.
questions.explanation: The NOTE says this pattern appears in almost all ConvNets, and p.265 describes information becoming 'increasingly contained in the channels'.

questions.question: What does layers.Rescaling(1.0 / 255) do to a pixel value of 51?
questions.answer: It maps it to 51 / 255 = 0.2.
questions.explanation: Rescaling multiplies inputs by the scale factor, mapping [0, 255] to [0, 1].

questions.question: Could you sketch the full dogs-vs-cats model from this page's description before reading p.270?
questions.answer: Input (180,180,3) → Rescaling → [Conv2D + MaxPooling2D] × 4 → Conv2D → GlobalAveragePooling2D → Dense(1, sigmoid), with filters growing from 32 to 512.
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with Listing 8.7 on p.270.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count 73,856 of conv2d_8.
questions.explanation: The layer receives 64 channels and has 128 filters of size 3x3, each with one bias.

questions.question: Why does max_pooling2d_3 output 43x43 rather than 43.5x43.5 or 44x44?
options: Pooling with stride 2 floors odd sizes, dropping the last row/column
The convolution added padding
Keras rounds up to the nearest odd number
The Rescaling layer cropped the image
questions.answer: Pooling with stride 2 floors odd sizes, dropping the last row/column
questions.explanation: 87/2 = 43.5 and only complete 2x2 windows are used, giving 43. No padding is used anywhere, Keras doesn't round to odd numbers, and Rescaling only changes pixel values, not shape.

questions.question: What does GlobalAveragePooling2D do to the (7, 7, 512) feature map, and how many parameters does it have?
questions.answer: It averages each of the 512 channels over the 7x7 spatial positions, producing a (512,) vector; it has 0 parameters.
questions.explanation: As the callout says, it flattens 3D activations into 1D by averaging over spatial dimensions; the summary shows Param # 0.

questions.question: How many parameters would the Dense(1) layer have if Flatten replaced GlobalAveragePooling2D, and why might that be worse for this small dataset?
questions.answer: 7·7·512 + 1 = 25,089 parameters; it would learn position-specific weights and be more prone to overfitting 2,000 training images.
questions.explanation: Flatten keeps all spatial positions as separate features. This comparison goes beyond the page but follows from the shapes it prints.

questions.question: Which layer has the most parameters?
options: conv2d_6 (32 filters)
conv2d_10 (512 filters)
dense_2
global_average_pooling2d_2
questions.answer: conv2d_10 (512 filters)
questions.explanation: 1,180,160 parameters, because it connects 256 input channels to 512 filters. conv2d_6 has 896, dense_2 has 513, and global pooling has none.

questions.question: Starting from 180x180, compute the spatial size after conv2d_9 and after max_pooling2d_5.
questions.answer: 18x18 after conv2d_9 and 9x9 after max_pooling2d_5.

questions.question: Without looking, can you reproduce the Output Shape column from the listing alone?
questions.answer: Self-check: apply −2 per conv and ÷2 (floor) per pool, channels = filter count.
questions.explanation: If you can, you understand how kernel size, padding and pooling govern shapes.

questions.question: Why is binary_crossentropy chosen in listing 8.8?
options: The model ends with a single sigmoid unit for a two-class problem
Adam only works with binary crossentropy
The images are binary (black and white)
The dataset has 2,000 training images
questions.answer: The model ends with a single sigmoid unit for a two-class problem
questions.explanation: The text ties the loss to the sigmoid output. Adam works with any differentiable loss, the images are RGB, and dataset size doesn't determine the loss.

questions.question: List the five preprocessing steps from JPEG files to model input.
questions.answer: Read the files; decode JPEG to RGB pixel grids; convert to floating-point tensors; resize to a shared size (180x180); pack into batches.
questions.explanation: These are the numbered steps of section 8.2.4.

questions.question: How does image_dataset_from_directory know the label of each image?
questions.answer: It treats each subdirectory of the given directory as a class and labels each image by the subdirectory it is in.
questions.explanation: The page: it lists the subdirectories and assumes each one contains images from one class.

questions.question: Show that 1,569,089 parameters correspond to the 5.99 MB in the summary.
questions.explanation: Each float32 weight occupies 4 bytes; Keras reports binary megabytes.

questions.question: Which batch size does listing 8.9 actually use?
questions.explanation: The code sets batch_size = 64, although the numbered list mentions 32; 180 is the image size and 16 does not appear.

questions.question: Why must images be resized to a shared size before batching?
questions.answer: A batch is a single rectangular tensor (batch, 180, 180, 3) and the model's input shape is fixed, so images of different sizes cannot be stacked or fed as-is.
questions.explanation: Follows from step 4 and the model's Input shape (p.269).

questions.question: Could you explain to someone what 'Non-trainable params: 0' means and when it would become non-zero?
questions.answer: No weights are frozen now; it becomes non-zero e.g. when a pretrained base is frozen (section 8.3) or with BatchNormalization statistics.
questions.explanation: Self-check of summary reading.

questions.question: What does tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(random_numbers) yield for random_numbers of shape (1000, 16)?
options: 1,000 elements of shape (16,)
One element of shape (1000, 16)
16 elements of shape (1000,)
Batches of 32 elements
questions.answer: 1,000 elements of shape (16,)
questions.explanation: It slices along the first axis, so each element is one sample; the page says the dataset yields single samples. It doesn't keep the whole array as one element, doesn't slice along the feature axis, and doesn't batch.

questions.question: Name two performance features of the Dataset class described on this page.
questions.answer: Parallelization of preprocessing across multiple CPU cores, and asynchronous data prefetching.
questions.explanation: Both are listed explicitly as features that would otherwise be cumbersome to implement.

questions.question: Explain in your own words what asynchronous prefetching achieves.
questions.answer: It prepares the next batch while the model is still processing the current one, so the model doesn't wait for data and execution flows without interruptions.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases the page's parenthetical definition.

questions.question: Which statement about using tf.data with Keras is correct according to the page?
options: It works the same with any Keras backend
It only works when the backend is TensorFlow
It must be converted to NumPy before calling fit()
It cannot be used in a Python for loop
questions.answer: It works the same with any Keras backend
questions.explanation: The page says it can be used with JAX or PyTorch and works the same independently of the backend; it can be passed directly to fit() and is an iterator usable in a for loop.

questions.question: What will a batch from train_dataset look like (shapes)?
questions.answer: images (64, 180, 180, 3) and labels (64,) — the last batch may be smaller.
questions.explanation: image_size=(180, 180), batch_size=64 (p.271), RGB images, one integer label each.

questions.question: Why are three separate datasets created rather than one?
questions.answer: Training data fit the weights, validation data monitor generalization during training and guide decisions, and the test data give a final unbiased estimate.
questions.explanation: The splits (2,000/1,000/2,000) were set up in section 8.2.2.

questions.question: Could you rewrite listing 8.10 so that the dataset yields (sample, label) pairs?
questions.answer: Pass a tuple: tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices((random_numbers, labels)).
questions.explanation: The callout notes from_tensor_slices accepts a tuple or dict of NumPy arrays.

questions.question: What shape do elements of dataset.batch(32) have for the toy dataset?
questions.explanation: Batching stacks 32 samples of shape (16,) along a new first axis. (16, 32) puts the axes in the wrong order, (16,) is unbatched, and (1000, 16) is the whole array.

questions.question: What does num_parallel_calls=8 do in listing 8.13?
questions.answer: It lets map process up to 8 elements concurrently, parallelizing the transformation across CPU cores.
questions.explanation: This is the parallel preprocessing feature described on p.272.

questions.question: Why does listing 8.13 print (4, 4) and not (32, 4, 4)?
questions.answer: map is applied to the original unbatched dataset, whose elements are (16,); batch() returned a separate dataset and did not modify dataset.
questions.explanation: Dataset methods return new datasets.

questions.question: Which method would you use to keep the GPU busy while the next batch is prepared?
options: .prefetch(buffer_size)
.shuffle(buffer_size)
.batch(32)
.map(callable)
questions.answer: .prefetch(buffer_size)
questions.explanation: The page says prefetch prepares a buffer of elements in GPU memory for better device utilization. Shuffle randomizes order, batch groups elements and map transforms them.

questions.question: How many batches does dataset.batch(32) produce for 1,000 samples, and what is the shape of the last one?
questions.answer: 32 batches: 31 of shape (32, 16) and a last one of shape (8, 16).
questions.explanation: 1,000 = 31·32 + 8; by default the remainder is kept. (Computation beyond the page.)

questions.question: What would go wrong if you used a shuffle buffer of size 10 on a dataset where all cat images come before all dog images?
questions.answer: Shuffling would only mix nearby elements, so batches would still be almost entirely cats early in the epoch and dogs later.
questions.explanation: shuffle works within a buffer; a small buffer gives only local randomness.

questions.question: Can you write a pipeline that shuffles, reshapes to (4, 4), batches by 32 and prefetches the toy dataset?
questions.answer: dataset.shuffle(1000).map(lambda x: tf.reshape(x, (4, 4)), num_parallel_calls=8).batch(32).prefetch(2)
questions.explanation: Chains the four methods introduced on the page.

questions.question: With save_best_only=True and monitor="val_loss", when does ModelCheckpoint write the file?
options: Only when val_loss is lower than at any previous epoch
After every epoch regardless of performance
Only at the end of training
When training accuracy reaches 100%
questions.answer: Only when val_loss is lower than at any previous epoch
questions.explanation: That is the condition stated on the page. Saving every epoch is the behavior without save_best_only; it doesn't wait for the end, and training accuracy isn't monitored.

questions.question: What are the shapes printed by listing 8.14, and what does each axis mean?
questions.answer: (32, 180, 180, 3): batch, height, width, RGB channels; (32,): one integer label per image.
questions.explanation: As printed; note listing 8.9 set batch_size = 64, which would give 64 in the first axis.

questions.question: Why does the checkpoint mean 'we won't have to retrain a new model for a lower number of epochs if we start overfitting'?
questions.answer: The file already contains the weights from the epoch with the best validation loss, i.e. the state before overfitting, so we can reload it instead of rerunning training with fewer epochs.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase of the page's reasoning.

questions.question: What role does validation_data=validation_dataset play in fit()?
options: It computes validation metrics at the end of each epoch
It is merged with the training data
It sets the learning rate
It shuffles the training data
questions.answer: It computes validation metrics at the end of each epoch
questions.explanation: The page: it monitors validation metrics on a separate Dataset. It is never used for training, and has nothing to do with the learning rate or shuffling.

questions.question: Given val_loss per epoch [0.70, 0.63, 0.65, 0.58, 0.60, 0.59], at which epochs does the callback save, and which epoch's model is in the file at the end?
questions.answer: Saves at epochs 1, 2 and 4; the file holds epoch 4 (val_loss 0.58).
questions.explanation: A save happens only when val_loss is a new minimum.

questions.question: After listing 8.15 finishes, which weights does the variable model contain, and what should you evaluate on the test set?
questions.answer: model contains the epoch-50 (likely overfit) weights; you should reload convnet_from_scratch.keras and evaluate that.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint is on disk; p.275 reloads it before evaluation.

questions.question: Can you explain why monitoring val_loss rather than training loss is necessary for picking the best model?
questions.answer: Training loss keeps decreasing even while the model overfits; only validation loss reflects generalization.
questions.explanation: Self-check linking this page to the overfitting curves on p.275.

questions.question: Which pattern in figure 8.9 indicates overfitting?
options: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss stops improving
Both losses decrease together until epoch 50
Validation accuracy exceeds training accuracy throughout
Training accuracy never exceeds 80%
questions.answer: Training loss keeps decreasing while validation loss stops improving
questions.explanation: That divergence is what the authors describe. Both losses do not keep decreasing together; validation accuracy is below training accuracy after the first epochs; training accuracy reaches nearly 100%.

questions.question: Around what value does the validation accuracy peak, according to the text?
questions.answer: Around 80%.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph below figure 8.9.

questions.question: Why do both loss curves start near 0.69?
questions.answer: An untrained model outputs about 0.5 for every image, and binary crossentropy at p = 0.5 is −ln 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
questions.explanation: The classes are balanced, so chance-level predictions give ln 2.

questions.question: Why do the authors reload the model from its saved file before measuring test accuracy?
questions.answer: The saved file holds the epoch with the lowest validation loss, i.e. the model before it started overfitting; the in-memory model is the overfit epoch-50 version.
questions.explanation: Follows from ModelCheckpoint(save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss") on p.274.

questions.question: In listing 8.16, what does plt.figure() do?
options: Starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately
Saves the accuracy plot to a file
Clears the history object
Displays the plots
questions.answer: Starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately
questions.explanation: It opens a fresh figure; saving would be plt.savefig, history is untouched, and plt.show() displays the plots.

questions.question: How can validation loss rise while validation accuracy stays around 80%?
questions.answer: The model becomes increasingly confident; its wrong predictions become very confident, and crossentropy penalizes them heavily, so average loss rises even if the number of correct predictions barely changes.
questions.explanation: An explanation beyond the page, consistent with figure 8.9.

questions.question: Looking at figure 8.9 yourself, at which epoch would you say the validation loss is lowest, and does it match the text's 'after only 10 epochs'?
questions.answer: In the printed figure the minimum looks closer to epochs 18–22 (~0.5); the text says 10. Either way, validation loss stops improving long before epoch 50.
questions.explanation: Practice reading curves critically; runs differ due to randomness.

questions.question: Why does Listing 8.17 reload the model from disk instead of evaluating the model that fit() just finished training?
questions.answer: The saved file holds the checkpoint with the best validation loss, from before overfitting set in; the in-memory model has the final, overfit weights.
questions.explanation: The previous page says the model is reloaded "to evaluate it as it was before it started overfitting". ModelCheckpoint saved only the best-validation epoch.

questions.question: Where does the book choose to apply data augmentation, and why?
options: Inside the model on the GPU, because it is always faster
In the data pipeline via Dataset.map() on the CPU, because it is usually the better option
On the test set, to make evaluation more robust
In a separate offline script that saves augmented images to disk
questions.answer: In the data pipeline via Dataset.map() on the CPU, because it is usually the better option
questions.explanation: The page says in-model augmentation can sometimes be faster but the pipeline is "usually the better option", so the chapter uses it. The GPU option is not always faster. Augmenting test data is wrong because augmentation is training-only. An offline script is not one of the two options given.

questions.question: The book says that with infinite data you would never overfit. Explain how data augmentation approximates this, and why it falls short.
questions.answer: It samples new, believable variants of existing images, so the model never sees an identical input and must learn transformation-invariant features. But the variants all derive from the same 2,000 originals, so they carry no fundamentally new information.
questions.explanation: The first part is from this page. The limitation is stated on p.278: inputs remain heavily intercorrelated, which is why dropout is added.

questions.question: Which transformation in Listing 8.18 would be inappropriate to swap for a vertical flip in the cats-vs-dogs task, and why?
options: RandomZoom, because zoom changes the image size
RandomFlip("horizontal"), because upside-down cats and dogs are not believable images
RandomRotation, because rotation needs a GPU
None, because all flips are equally valid
questions.answer: RandomFlip("horizontal"), because upside-down cats and dogs are not believable images
questions.explanation: The page requires transformations that "yield believable-looking images". A mirror image of a pet is realistic, but an upside-down one is not. The other options misstate what the layers do, or ignore the believability requirement.

questions.question: What are the two earlier anti-overfitting techniques the page names, and what distinguishes augmentation from them?
questions.answer: Dropout and weight decay (L2 regularization). Those constrain the model, while augmentation is specific to computer vision and works on the training data.
questions.explanation: Dropout and weight decay are listed on the page. The model-versus-data contrast is our reading of the text, which calls augmentation "specific to computer vision".

questions.question: If you place augmentation layers inside the model, will they distort the test accuracy computed by evaluate()? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Keras random augmentation layers are active only in training mode and act as the identity during evaluate() and predict().
questions.explanation: The book later stresses that evaluation uses non-augmented images (p.278). Keras's training flag ensures this automatically for in-model layers.

questions.question: Can you sketch the data flow for both augmentation placements, say which hardware runs each, and say where the Rescaling layer sits relative to the augmentation layers?
questions.answer: In-model: batches go to the augmentation layers, then Rescaling, then the convnet, all on the GPU. Pipeline: train_dataset.map(augment) runs on parallel CPU cores and feeds a model that starts at Rescaling.
questions.explanation: Compare your sketch with the two bullets and the following paragraph on this page.

questions.question: What rotation range in degrees would RandomRotation(0.05) produce? And RandomRotation(0.25)?
questions.answer: ±18° and ±90° respectively.
questions.explanation: The factor is a fraction of a full circle: 0.05 × 360° = 18° and 0.25 × 360° = 90°, by the same reasoning the page uses to turn 0.1 into ±36°.

questions.question: What is the role of `prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)` in this code?
options: It applies the augmentation layers on the GPU
It prepares upcoming batches ahead of time so the GPU does not wait, which is important for best performance
It caches augmented images so that each epoch sees the same augmentations
It shuffles the dataset
questions.answer: It prepares upcoming batches ahead of time so the GPU does not wait, which is important for best performance
questions.explanation: The callout says it "enables prefetching of batches on GPU memory; important for best performance". It does not move augmentation to the GPU (map does the augmentation on CPU threads), it does not cache results (augmentations differ each epoch), and it does not shuffle.

questions.question: Why does the data_augmentation function return `targets` unchanged?
questions.answer: The transformations preserve the label (a flipped, rotated or zoomed dog is still a dog), and fit() needs (input, target) pairs.
questions.explanation: Augmentation must yield believable images of the same class (p.276), so only the images change.

questions.question: On average, how many images in a batch of 32 are horizontally flipped, and why is a vertical flip not used?
questions.answer: About 16. Vertical flips would produce upside-down animals, which are not believable images of the classes.
questions.explanation: RandomFlip("horizontal") flips a random 50% of images. The believability criterion comes from p.276.

questions.question: Which dataset(s) should the `data_augmentation` map be applied to?
options: train_dataset only
train_dataset and validation_dataset
All three splits
test_dataset only
questions.answer: train_dataset only
questions.explanation: Only train_dataset is mapped on this page, and p.278 states that evaluation uses non-augmented images because augmentation is a training-time regularizer. Augmenting validation or test data would distort the generalization estimate.

questions.question: In Figure 8.10, some panels have mirrored or smeared strips along the edges. What causes them?
questions.answer: Rotation and zoom-out expose regions outside the original image, and the layers fill them with pixels derived from the image border (a reflection fill).
questions.explanation: This is our inference from the figure. The page does not discuss fill modes, but the artifacts are consistent with Keras's default reflective filling.

questions.question: Can you rewrite the augmentation stage using `keras.Sequential(data_augmentation_layers)` instead of the explicit loop, and explain why the result is equivalent?
questions.answer: aug = keras.Sequential(data_augmentation_layers); train_dataset.map(lambda x, y: (aug(x), y), num_parallel_calls=8). Sequential calls the layers in order, which is exactly what the loop does.
questions.explanation: Both apply flip, rotate and zoom in sequence to the images and leave the targets untouched.

questions.question: Why do the authors add Dropout even though augmentation guarantees the model never sees the same input twice?
options: Because augmentation slows down training
Because augmented inputs are heavily intercorrelated, as they are remixes of a small number of originals
Because Dropout is required whenever GlobalAveragePooling2D is used
Because augmentation only works on the GPU
questions.answer: Because augmented inputs are heavily intercorrelated, as they are remixes of a small number of originals
questions.explanation: The page states that augmentation "can't produce new information", so it may not fully prevent overfitting. The other options are not reasons given and are not true requirements.

questions.question: In Listing 8.19, what does `train_dataset.take(1)` do, and why is the plain train_dataset used instead of augmented_train_dataset?
questions.answer: It yields only the first batch (like breaking after one iteration). The plain dataset is used so the same original image can be augmented nine different ways by explicit calls to data_augmentation.
questions.explanation: The callout explains take(N), and the second callout says each iteration is a different augmentation of the same image.

questions.question: Compute the spatial size of the feature maps just before GlobalAveragePooling2D in Listing 8.20, starting from 180×180.
questions.explanation: Each unpadded 3×3 conv subtracts 2 and each 2×2 pool halves, rounding down. This matches the 7×7 stated on p.269.

questions.question: How many trainable parameters does the final Dense(1) layer have, and does Dropout(0.25) add any?
questions.answer: 513 (512 weights + 1 bias). Dropout has no parameters.
questions.explanation: The input to Dense is the 512-vector from global average pooling (unchanged in shape by dropout).

questions.question: Why does the book double the number of training epochs to 100, and why evaluate on unaugmented images?
questions.answer: With augmentation and dropout, overfitting is expected to occur much later, so the best epoch lies later. Evaluation uses clean images because augmentation is a training-time regularization technique, and metrics should reflect real data.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are stated in the last paragraph of the page. p.279 confirms overfitting starts around epochs 60–70.

questions.question: Where exactly is the Dropout layer inserted in Listing 8.20?
options: Right after Rescaling
Between every Conv2D and MaxPooling2D
Between GlobalAveragePooling2D and the Dense(1) classifier
After the sigmoid output
questions.answer: Between GlobalAveragePooling2D and the Dense(1) classifier
questions.explanation: The text says "right before the densely connected classifier", and the code confirms it. The other placements do not appear in the listing, and dropout after the output would corrupt the predictions.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write down the full layer list of Listing 8.20 with filter counts and explain what each regularizer (augmentation, dropout) contributes?
questions.answer: Rescaling; Conv 32/64/128/256/512 with MaxPool after the first four; GlobalAveragePooling2D; Dropout(0.25); Dense(1, sigmoid). Augmentation diversifies the inputs, and dropout keeps the classifier from depending on specific features.
questions.explanation: Check your answer against the listing and the paragraph above it.

questions.question: According to the authors, when does the regularized model start overfitting?
options: Around epoch 10
Around epochs 30–40
Around epochs 60–70
It never overfits within 100 epochs
questions.answer: Around epochs 60–70
questions.explanation: The text says "around epochs 60–70 (compared to epoch 10 for the original model)". Epoch 10 is the baseline. The claim that it never overfits is contradicted by the widening gap in Figure 8.11.

questions.question: Why does Listing 8.21 use a different checkpoint filename from the baseline run?
questions.answer: So the best regularized model is saved separately without overwriting convnet_from_scratch.keras, and both can be evaluated and compared (and the new one reused in the next chapter).
questions.explanation: The two listings use distinct filenames. p.280 mentions reusing the augmentation checkpoint later.

questions.question: In Figure 8.11, validation loss is very noisy after about epoch 40 while training loss falls smoothly. How does the training setup protect you from this noise?
questions.answer: ModelCheckpoint with monitor="val_loss" and save_best_only=True keeps the epoch with the lowest validation loss, and Listing 8.22 reloads that checkpoint instead of using the final weights.
questions.explanation: Since the last epoch may fall on a spike (for example the near-0.8 value around epoch 98), selecting the best epoch matters.

questions.question: Which dataset is passed as validation_data in Listing 8.21?
options: augmented_train_dataset
validation_dataset (unaugmented)
test_dataset
An augmented copy of validation_dataset
questions.answer: validation_dataset (unaugmented)
questions.explanation: Augmentation is applied only at training time (p.278). Using the training data or the test set for validation would bias model selection, and augmenting validation data would misrepresent real inputs.

questions.question: The regularized model's final training accuracy (about 95%) is lower than the baseline's (nearly 100%), yet it is the better model. Explain.
questions.answer: Augmentation and dropout make the training task harder and prevent memorization. That lowers training fit but improves generalization, which is what validation and test accuracy measure (above 85% validation, 83.9% test, against about 80% and 78.6%).
questions.explanation: Generalization, not training fit, is the goal. Compare Figure 8.9 (p.275) with Figure 8.11.

questions.question: Can you sketch Figure 8.11 from memory, marking where the accuracy curves separate and where validation loss stops improving, and say how this differs from Figure 8.9?
questions.answer: The accuracy curves stay together until about epoch 40, then validation plateaus at roughly 0.8–0.87 while training climbs to about 0.95. Validation loss bottoms out around 0.4 and turns noisy. In the baseline, separation happened around epoch 10.
questions.explanation: Check your sketch against the figure on this page and on p.275.

questions.question: What test accuracy does the regularized from-scratch model achieve, and what ceiling do the authors estimate for further from-scratch tuning?
questions.answer: 83.9%, with a likely ceiling of about 90%.
questions.explanation: Both figures are stated in the first two paragraphs of the page.

questions.question: Why do the authors say it would be difficult to exceed about 90% by training your own convnet from scratch?
options: Because Keras limits model size
Because you have so little data to work with
Because convnets cannot classify animals
Because data augmentation stops working after 100 epochs
questions.answer: Because you have so little data to work with
questions.explanation: The text attributes the limit to the small dataset. Keras imposes no such size limit, convnets classify animals fine, and nothing is said about augmentation failing after 100 epochs.

questions.question: What condition must the original training dataset satisfy for a pretrained model's features to act as a "generic model of the visual world"?
questions.answer: It must be large enough and general enough, as ImageNet is with 1.4 million images in 1,000 diverse classes.
questions.explanation: The page states the condition explicitly. A narrow or small source dataset would produce features specific to that domain.

questions.question: In feature extraction as defined on this page, which part is trained from scratch?
options: The entire pretrained network
The convolutional base only
A new classifier that takes the extracted features as input
Nothing; feature extraction requires no training
questions.answer: A new classifier that takes the extracted features as input
questions.explanation: The features are "run through a new classifier, which is trained from scratch." Training the base corresponds to fine-tuning or training from scratch, and some training is always required.

questions.question: The authors use a furniture-recognition example. What point does it illustrate, and why is the dogs-vs-cats case easier than that example?
questions.answer: It shows that learned features transfer even to classes absent from the source dataset. Dogs vs. cats is easier because ImageNet already contains many cat and dog species, so the source and target overlap.
questions.explanation: Both points are on this page. p.285 notes the resulting comparison is "a bit unfair".

questions.question: What are the two parts of an image-classification convnet, and what is the first part called?
questions.answer: A series of convolution and pooling layers followed by a densely connected classifier. The first part is the convolutional base, or backbone.
questions.explanation: This is stated in the last paragraph of the page, which continues on p.281.

questions.question: Can you explain, in your own words, why portability of learned features is a key advantage of deep learning over older shallow approaches?
questions.answer: Deep models learn their own hierarchical features from data, and those features (edges, textures, parts) are useful across tasks. Shallow approaches rely on task-specific engineered features or learn nothing reusable.
questions.explanation: The page makes the claim about portability. The contrast with engineered features is our elaboration.

questions.question: In Figure 8.12's right-hand panel, what is the state of each component?
options: Base trainable, classifier pretrained
Base frozen (pretrained), classifier new and randomly initialized
Both frozen
Both randomly initialized
questions.answer: Base frozen (pretrained), classifier new and randomly initialized
questions.explanation: The labels read "Trained convolutional base (frozen)" and "New classifier (randomly initialized)". The other combinations describe fine-tuning, inference only, or training from scratch.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors give for not reusing the densely connected classifier.
questions.answer: (1) Its representations are specific to the original classes and encode only per-class presence probabilities for the whole picture. (2) Dense layers discard spatial information about where objects are.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are stated in the main paragraph. The convolutional feature maps, by contrast, are generic and spatial.

questions.question: What does it mean that a convnet's feature maps are "presence maps of generic concepts over a picture"?
questions.answer: Each channel of a feature map indicates, at each spatial location, how strongly a learned pattern (an edge, texture or part) is present. That information is useful for many vision tasks, not just the original classes.
questions.explanation: This is the authors' justification for reusing the base. The phrase combines genericity (the concepts) with spatial structure (over a picture).

questions.question: You want to classify microscope images of cells using an ImageNet-pretrained convnet. Following this page's advice, what should you consider?
options: Reusing the entire network including the ImageNet classifier
Using only the first few layers of the convolutional base for feature extraction
Using only the deepest layers, because they are the most abstract
Avoiding pretrained models entirely
questions.answer: Using only the first few layers of the convolutional base for feature extraction
questions.explanation: When the new dataset differs a lot from the original, early generic layers (edges, colors, textures) transfer better than deep abstract ones such as "cat ear". The ImageNet classifier is class-specific. The page does not advise abandoning pretraining.

questions.question: Why are densely connected features "largely useless" for problems where object location matters?
questions.answer: Dense layers mix all spatial positions into a single vector and so remove the notion of space. Convolutional feature maps still record where patterns occur.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly on the page, and it is why location-sensitive tasks rely on convolutional backbones.

questions.question: Can you redraw Figure 8.12 from memory and annotate which parts are trained, frozen, discarded or new?
questions.answer: Left: trained base and trained classifier. Middle: the trained classifier is crossed out. Right: the trained base (frozen) with a new classifier (randomly initialized).
questions.explanation: Compare your drawing with the figure. The key point is that the base carries over unchanged.

questions.question: Why do the authors avoid reusing Xception's original densely connected classifier for the dogs-vs-cats task?
options: Because ImageNet contains no dog or cat classes
To demonstrate the general case where the new classes do not overlap the original class set
Because dense layers cannot be loaded from KerasHub
Because the dense head has too many parameters to fit in memory
questions.answer: To demonstrate the general case where the new classes do not overlap the original class set
questions.explanation: The page states that reusing the dense layers would likely be beneficial (ImageNet has several dog and cat classes) but they choose not to so as to cover the general case. Option 1 contradicts the text; options 3 and 4 are not mentioned and are false (KerasHub can load full models, see p.324).

questions.question: What does each part of the preset name `xception_41_imagenet` indicate?
questions.answer: `xception` is the architecture family, `41` is the depth (41 trainable conv and dense layers), and `imagenet` is the dataset the weights were trained on.
questions.explanation: The page explains the 41 as the count of trainable layers and states the model is Xception trained on ImageNet.

questions.question: Explain why feeding images with pixel values in [0, 1] to a model pretrained on [-1, 1] inputs is harmful, and how KerasHub avoids the issue.
questions.answer: The pretrained weights are tuned to the input distribution seen in pretraining; a different range shifts and scales every activation, so the learned features no longer fire correctly and the model would have to relearn feature extraction. KerasHub's `ImageConverter.from_preset()` applies the rescaling that matches the checkpoint.
questions.explanation: Directly from the last paragraph of the page; the alternative of manually tracking each model's range is what ImageConverter replaces.

questions.question: In KerasHub terminology, what is a 'backbone'?
options: The full pretrained model including the classification head
The preprocessing layer that rescales images
The feature-extractor network without the classification head
The downloaded weight file
questions.answer: The feature-extractor network without the classification head
questions.explanation: The page defines backbone as the underlying feature extractor network without the classification head (= convolutional base). The full model with head is a 'task' (p.324); preprocessing is ImageConverter; weights are part of the preset.

questions.question: When might you reuse only the first few layers of a pretrained model instead of the whole convolutional base?
questions.answer: When the new dataset differs a lot from the dataset the original model was trained on, since only early layers' generic features (edges, colors, textures) transfer well.
questions.explanation: The page's opening sentence, completing the argument from p.281 about layer generality.

questions.question: What does `from_preset()` do when called on `keras_hub.models.Backbone`?
options: Trains Xception from scratch on ImageNet
Downloads the configuration and weights for the named model and builds it
Only downloads the weights; the architecture must be defined manually
Converts a Keras model into a preset file
questions.answer: Downloads the configuration and weights for the named model and builds it
questions.explanation: The page says it downloads the configuration and weights. No training happens (option 1), the architecture comes from the configuration (option 3), and it loads rather than saves (option 4).

questions.question: Without looking, write the two lines of Listing 8.23 and state what you must install first if you are not on Colab or Kaggle.
questions.answer: `import keras_hub` and `conv_base = keras_hub.models.Backbone.from_preset("xception_41_imagenet")`; install with `pip install keras-hub`.
questions.explanation: Checks recall of the listing and the NOTE about KerasHub being a separate package.

questions.question: Why does the fast feature-extraction technique not allow data augmentation?
options: Because NumPy arrays cannot store image data
Because the convolutional base is run only once per input image, so no new random variants are seen
Because the Xception backbone rejects augmented images
Because Dense layers cannot be trained on augmented data
questions.answer: Because the convolutional base is run only once per input image, so no new random variants are seen
questions.explanation: The page says the technique is cheap because the base runs once per image, 'but for the same reason' it won't allow augmentation. The other options are false: NumPy stores features fine, Xception accepts any properly preprocessed image, and Dense layers can be trained on any features.

questions.question: What two arguments are passed to `ImageConverter.from_preset()` in Listing 8.24 and what does each control?
questions.answer: The preset name `"xception_41_imagenet"`, which selects the rescaling that matches Xception's pretraining, and `image_size=(180, 180)`, which sets the output image size.
questions.explanation: Taken directly from Listing 8.24; the preset must be the same one used for the backbone.
