questions.question: Why is end-to-end feature extraction 'far more expensive' even when the convolutional base is not being updated?
questions.answer: Because every input image goes through the large convolutional base every time it is seen, i.e., once per epoch, instead of once in total.
questions.explanation: The page states this is the same reason it allows augmentation; the base is by far the most expensive part of the pipeline.

questions.question: In Listing 8.25, what does `np.concatenate(all_features)` do?
options: Averages features across batches
Joins the list of per-batch feature arrays into one array along the sample axis
Flattens each feature map into a vector
Concatenates features with labels
questions.answer: Joins the list of per-batch feature arrays into one array along the sample axis
questions.explanation: `np.concatenate` joins along axis 0 by default, stacking batches into one array of all samples. It does not average, flatten, or combine with labels (labels are concatenated separately).

questions.question: If the backbone forward pass dominates cost and you train the classifier for 30 epochs, roughly how many times more backbone forward passes does end-to-end feature extraction require than cached feature extraction?
questions.answer: About 30 times more (N x 30 versus N).
questions.explanation: Cached extraction runs the base once per image; end-to-end runs it once per image per epoch. This is an AI-derived estimate consistent with the page's qualitative statement.

questions.question: Why does `get_features_and_labels` call `preprocessor(images)` before `conv_base.predict`?
questions.answer: To rescale and resize the images exactly as Xception's pretraining expects; otherwise the pretrained features would not apply.
questions.explanation: Follows from p.282: inputs must match the checkpoint's input range, which ImageConverter enforces.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone, in two sentences each, the pros and cons of the two feature-extraction options on this page?
questions.answer: Option 1: cheap and fast because the base runs once; no augmentation. Option 2: supports augmentation because images pass through the base each time; far more expensive.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the central comparison of the page.

questions.question: What does GlobalAveragePooling2D do to the (6, 6, 2048) feature tensor in Listing 8.26?
options: Reshapes it into a 73,728-dimensional vector
Averages over the 6x6 spatial positions, producing a 2,048-dimensional vector
Takes the maximum over channels, producing a 6x6 map
Applies a learned 1x1 convolution
questions.answer: Averages over the 6x6 spatial positions, producing a 2,048-dimensional vector
questions.explanation: The callout says it averages spatial dimensions to flatten the feature map. Option 1 describes Flatten; option 3 pools over the wrong axis with max; option 4 would add weights, but GAP has none.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters in the model of Listing 8.26.
questions.answer: Dense(256): 2048*256 + 256 = 524,544; Dense(1): 256 + 1 = 257; total 524,801 (pooling and dropout have none).
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has inputs x units weights plus units biases; GlobalAveragePooling2D outputs 2,048 values.

questions.question: Why does the feature-extraction loop in Listing 8.25 separate labels from images?
questions.answer: Because predict() only expects images, but the dataset yields (images, labels) batches; the labels are collected separately to stay aligned with the features.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sentence of the page.

questions.question: What does the ModelCheckpoint callback in Listing 8.26 save?
options: The model after every epoch to separate files
Only the model with the lowest validation loss seen so far
Only the model with the highest training accuracy
The extracted features
questions.answer: Only the model with the lowest validation loss seen so far
questions.explanation: save_best_only=True with monitor="val_loss" overwrites feature_extraction.keras only when val_loss improves. It does not save every epoch, does not use training accuracy, and does not save features.

questions.question: Why is an epoch so fast here compared with the from-scratch ConvNet of section 8.2?
questions.answer: Because the convolutional work was done once during feature extraction; training only involves two Dense layers on 2,048-dimensional vectors, so an epoch takes under a second even on CPU.
questions.explanation: The page attributes the speed to dealing with only two Dense layers.

questions.question: What does the shape (2000, 6, 6, 2048) tell you about each training image's representation?
questions.answer: There are 2,000 images; each is described by a 6x6 grid of positions, each position holding a 2,048-dimensional feature vector.
questions.explanation: Interpretation of the printed train_features.shape.

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 8.26 from memory and justify each of its five layers?
questions.answer: Input(6,6,2048); GlobalAveragePooling2D to collapse space; Dense(256, relu) for a hidden representation; Dropout(0.25) to regularize; Dense(1, sigmoid) for the binary probability.
questions.explanation: Self-check on the structure of the head.

questions.question: Why do the authors call the comparison with the from-scratch model 'a bit unfair'?
options: The pretrained model was trained for more epochs on dogs vs. cats
ImageNet contains many dog and cat instances, so the pretrained model already has the required knowledge
The from-scratch model used a smaller image size
The validation set was different
questions.answer: ImageNet contains many dog and cat instances, so the pretrained model already has the required knowledge
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the text. The pretrained base was never trained on this dataset (option 1), and image size and validation split are not the reason given (options 3 and 4).

questions.question: What in figure 8.13 indicates overfitting, and what cause do the authors give?
questions.answer: Training accuracy goes to ~100% and training loss to ~0 within a few epochs while validation loss stays around 0.08-0.13 and fluctuates; the cause is the lack of data augmentation, essential with small image datasets.
questions.explanation: The text says the plots indicate overfitting almost from the start despite dropout, because the technique doesn't use augmentation.

questions.question: Which model is evaluated on the test set, and why that one?
questions.answer: The model reloaded from feature_extraction.keras, i.e., the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss saved by ModelCheckpoint, because it is the best model before overfitting got worse.
questions.explanation: The checkpoint was configured with save_best_only=True and monitor="val_loss" on p.284.

questions.question: In Listing 8.27, what is the purpose of `plt.figure()`?
options: It saves the first plot to disk
It starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately from the accuracy curves
It clears the history object
It displays the legend
questions.answer: It starts a new figure so the loss curves are drawn separately from the accuracy curves
questions.explanation: plt.figure() creates a new figure; saving needs plt.savefig, history is untouched, and legends come from plt.legend().

questions.question: Why didn't Dropout(0.25) prevent overfitting here?
questions.answer: Because the inputs (cached features) are identical every epoch; without augmentation the head can still memorize the small training set. The authors say augmentation is essential for small image datasets.
questions.explanation: Book states the cause; the mechanism detail is an AI explanation.

questions.question: Can you sketch, from memory, the general shape of the four curves in figure 8.13 and explain what each tells you?
questions.answer: Train acc rises to 1.0; val acc plateaus ~0.98; train loss drops to ~0; val loss fluctuates ~0.08-0.13. Together: strong features, early overfitting.
questions.explanation: Self-check on figure reading.

questions.question: Why must the convolutional base be frozen before training the new classifier end to end?
options: To make the forward pass faster
Because the randomly initialized Dense layers would propagate very large weight updates that destroy the learned representations
Because Keras cannot backpropagate through KerasHub models
To make data augmentation possible
questions.answer: Because the randomly initialized Dense layers would propagate very large weight updates that destroy the learned representations
questions.explanation: That is the reason given on the page. Freezing does not speed up the forward pass, Keras can backpropagate through backbones (fine-tuning does), and augmentation is enabled by the end-to-end setup, not by freezing.

questions.question: What does Listing 8.29 print before and after freezing, and what does that demonstrate?
questions.answer: 26 trainable weights with trainable=True and 0 with trainable=False, demonstrating that freezing empties the trainable weights list.
questions.explanation: Directly from the listing and the sentence preceding it.

questions.question: Give two ways to freeze the Xception backbone shown on this page.
questions.answer: Pass `trainable=False` to `Backbone.from_preset(...)` (Listing 8.28), or set `conv_base.trainable = False` (Listing 8.29).
questions.explanation: Both appear on the page.

questions.question: Why does the new model take inputs of shape (180, 180, 3) instead of (6, 6, 2048) as in Listing 8.26?
questions.answer: Because the backbone is now part of the model; raw (possibly augmented) images enter, are preprocessed and pass through the frozen base on every step, which is what allows data augmentation.
questions.explanation: Contrasts option 1 (cached features) with option 2 (end to end) from p.283.

questions.question: What was the test accuracy of the fast feature-extraction model?
questions.explanation: Stated in the first sentence. 84% is the from-scratch target (p.266), 98.4% is the augmented feature-extraction result (p.288), and 98.6% is the fine-tuned result (p.290).

questions.question: In the new model, how many trainable scalar parameters are there, given the backbone is frozen and Dense(256) receives 2,048 inputs?
questions.explanation: Same head as Listing 8.26; frozen backbone contributes zero trainable parameters. p.287 confirms only four weight tensors (two kernels, two biases) are trained.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, what would happen in the first few training steps if you forgot to freeze conv_base?
questions.answer: The random head would produce large errors; their gradients would flow into Xception and apply large, uninformative updates that erase its pretrained features.
questions.explanation: Self-check of the page's central argument.

questions.question: How many weight tensors are trained in the frozen-base model, and why?
options: 26, the backbone's weights
4, a weight matrix and a bias vector for each of the two Dense layers
2, one per Dense layer
30, one per epoch
questions.answer: 4, a weight matrix and a bias vector for each of the two Dense layers
questions.explanation: The page says four weight tensors, two per layer. 26 is the backbone count before freezing (p.286), which is now 0; option 3 forgets biases; option 4 confuses tensors with epochs.

questions.question: What must you do if you change a layer's trainable attribute after compiling the model?
questions.answer: Recompile the model; otherwise the change is ignored.
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page.

questions.question: Why can this model be trained for 30 epochs while the cached-feature head was trained for only 10?
questions.answer: Data augmentation makes the model see different image variants each epoch, so overfitting starts much later; the cached head overfit almost immediately.
questions.explanation: The page attributes the longer training to augmentation delaying overfitting; p.285 showed early overfitting without it.

questions.question: Why does the book say this technique is intractable on CPU?
options: Because Adam cannot run on CPU
Because every image passes through the large Xception base on every epoch
Because data augmentation is only implemented on GPU
Because the head has millions of parameters
questions.answer: Because every image passes through the large Xception base on every epoch
questions.explanation: The cost comes from repeated forward passes of the convolutional base (p.283). Adam and augmentation run on CPU; the head has only about 525k parameters.

questions.question: In Listing 8.30, why is `evaluate` called on `test_dataset` rather than on `test_features`?
questions.answer: Because this model contains the preprocessor and the frozen backbone, so it takes raw images; the cached test_features were only needed for the standalone head of Listing 8.26.
questions.explanation: Contrasts this listing with the evaluation on p.285.

questions.question: List the shapes of the four trainable tensors and compute the total number of trainable scalars.
questions.explanation: Follows from the Dense layer sizes after GlobalAveragePooling2D outputs 2,048 features.

questions.question: Could you decide, given only a CPU laptop, which of the two feature-extraction techniques to use, and justify it with the book's arguments?
questions.answer: The cached-feature technique: the book says end-to-end with augmentation is intractable on CPU, while cached features train in under a second per epoch.
questions.explanation: Self-check combining the NOTE on this page with p.284.

questions.question: Why must the classifier on top be trained before the convolutional base is unfrozen for fine-tuning?
options: Because Keras cannot compute gradients for frozen layers.
Because an untrained classifier produces a large error signal that would destroy the base's learned representations.
Because training the classifier first reduces the number of parameters in the base.
Because the base cannot be unfrozen once it has been compiled.
questions.answer: Because an untrained classifier produces a large error signal that would destroy the base's learned representations.
questions.explanation: The page states that with an untrained classifier the error signal propagating through the network is too large and the representations of the layers being fine-tuned are destroyed. The other options are false: gradients can flow through frozen layers, training the head does not change the base's parameter count, and trainability can be changed after compile (followed by recompiling, p.287).

questions.question: List the five steps of fine-tuning in order, and say which of them were already completed during feature extraction.
questions.answer: 1 Add custom network on top of a trained base; 2 freeze the base; 3 train the added part; 4 unfreeze the base; 5 jointly train base and added part. Steps 1-3 were done in feature extraction.
questions.explanation: The list is on this page; p.289 states that the first three steps were already completed when doing feature extraction.

questions.question: Feature extraction with data augmentation reached 98.4% test accuracy, no better than without augmentation. What explanation do the authors offer, and what does it tell you about augmentation in general?
questions.answer: The augmentation configuration may not exactly match the distribution of the test data. Augmentation only helps if the transformations produce variation that the model will actually encounter at test time.
questions.explanation: The authors' hypothesis is stated on the page. The general lesson (inferred) is that augmentation is a modeling assumption about invariances in the data, not a free improvement.

questions.question: In figure 8.14, validation accuracy is about 98% at epoch 1 while training accuracy is about 93%. Why is this not a sign of a bug?
questions.answer: The frozen pretrained features are already very good, so the head learns quickly; training metrics are measured on augmented images with dropout active, which are harder than the clean validation images.
questions.explanation: Augmentation (p.276) and dropout act only in training, so training metrics underestimate the model's performance on clean data. This is an AI explanation consistent with the figure.

questions.question: Why is the technique called fine-tuning?
options: Because it tunes the hyperparameters of the model with a fine grid search.
Because it trains only the final layer of the network.
Because it slightly adjusts the more abstract representations of the reused model to make them more relevant to the new problem.
Because it uses a finer image resolution than feature extraction.
questions.answer: Because it slightly adjusts the more abstract representations of the reused model to make them more relevant to the new problem.
questions.explanation: This is the book's definition. Fine-tuning is not hyperparameter search, it trains the base as well as the head (not just the final layer), and it has nothing to do with image resolution.

questions.question: Without looking, explain to yourself the difference between feature extraction and fine-tuning in terms of which weights the optimizer updates in each case.
questions.answer: Feature extraction: only the new head's weights are updated; the base is frozen. Fine-tuning: after the head is trained, the base (or part of it) is unfrozen and both base and head weights are updated together.
questions.explanation: Check your answer against the definition on this page and the description of freezing on p.286.

questions.question: What does `for layer in conv_base.layers[:-4]: layer.trainable = False` do after `conv_base.trainable = True`?
options: Freezes the last four layers and trains the rest.
Leaves only the last four layers of the base trainable.
Removes the last four layers from the model.
Freezes every fourth layer of the base.
questions.answer: Leaves only the last four layers of the base trainable.
questions.explanation: layers[:-4] is every layer except the last four; those get frozen, so only the top four remain trainable. It doesn't remove layers, doesn't freeze the last four (that would be layers[-4:]), and isn't a stride (that would be layers[::4]).

questions.question: Give the two reasons from the sidebar for fine-tuning only the top layers of a convolutional base.
questions.answer: (1) Lower layers encode generic, reusable features while higher layers encode specialized ones that need repurposing, so fine-tuning lower layers gives fast-decreasing returns. (2) More trainable parameters means more overfitting risk; the base has 15 million parameters, too many for a small dataset.
questions.explanation: Both bullets in the 'Partial fine-tuning' sidebar.

questions.question: Why does fine-tuning use a very low learning rate such as 1e-5?
questions.answer: To limit the magnitude of the modifications made to the representations being fine-tuned; large updates may harm those pretrained representations.
questions.explanation: Stated directly before Listing 8.31. The pretrained weights are already good, so you only want small adjustments.

questions.question: Which layers does the book say you should NOT unfreeze when fine-tuning?
options: Dense layers
Conv2D layers in the top block
BatchNormalization layers
Dropout layers
questions.answer: BatchNormalization layers
questions.explanation: The page says explicitly not to unfreeze BatchNormalization layers; chapter 9 explains why (p.302). Dense and top Conv2D layers are exactly what you train; Dropout has no weights.

questions.question: Listing 8.31 calls model.compile again. Why is recompiling necessary at this point?
questions.answer: Because trainability was changed (the base was unfrozen); in Keras such changes only take effect after recompiling. Recompiling also creates the optimizer with the new, low learning rate.
questions.explanation: p.287 states that if you modify weight trainability after compilation you must recompile, or the changes are ignored.

questions.question: What does the ModelCheckpoint callback in Listing 8.31 save, and when?
questions.answer: It saves the model to fine_tuning.keras at the end of an epoch only when val_loss improves (save_best_only=True, monitor="val_loss"), so the file holds the best epoch.
questions.explanation: The file is loaded back for test evaluation on p.290.

questions.question: Could you write, from memory, the code to unfreeze a pretrained base, keep its BatchNormalization layers frozen, and recompile with a learning rate of 1e-5?
questions.answer: Set conv_base.trainable = True, loop over conv_base.layers and set trainable = False for BatchNormalization instances, then model.compile(..., optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=1e-5), ...).
questions.explanation: Compare with the sidebar snippet and Listing 8.31; the BN loop is an AI-written combination of the book's advice.

questions.question: Why does the evaluation code call keras.models.load_model("fine_tuning.keras") before evaluate?
options: Because fit deletes the model from memory.
To evaluate the epoch with the lowest validation loss rather than the last epoch.
To reset the base to its pretrained ImageNet weights.
Because evaluate only works on models loaded from disk.
questions.answer: To evaluate the epoch with the lowest validation loss rather than the last epoch.
questions.explanation: ModelCheckpoint with save_best_only=True and monitor="val_loss" (p.289) writes the best epoch to that file. fit does not delete the model, loading does not restore ImageNet weights, and evaluate works on any compiled model.

questions.question: What test accuracy does fine-tuning reach, and how much variation do the authors say to expect?
questions.answer: 98.6%, with your own results possibly within half a percentage point.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after figure 8.15.

questions.question: Why do the authors say the comparison with the original Kaggle competition is 'not quite a fair comparison'?
questions.answer: Because the pretrained features already contained prior knowledge about cats and dogs (ImageNet has many such images), which competitors couldn't use at the time.
questions.explanation: The page gives this reason; p.285 notes ImageNet contains many dog and cat instances.

questions.question: The test set has 2,000 images (p.265). Roughly how many images does a 98.6% model misclassify, and how many more does a 98.4% model misclassify?
questions.answer: About 28 errors at 98.6% (1.4% of 2,000); about 32 at 98.4%; so about 4 more images.
questions.explanation: $0.014 \times 2000 = 28$ and $0.016 \times 2000 = 32$. A 4-image difference is smaller than the ±0.5-point (±10 images) variance the authors mention.

questions.question: In figure 8.15 training accuracy is above validation accuracy, whereas in figure 8.14 it was mostly below. What changed?
questions.answer: The base is now trainable, so the model adapts its features to the training images and fits them slightly better than unseen validation images; with a frozen base, the harder augmented training inputs kept training accuracy below validation.
questions.explanation: An interpretation of the two figures (p.288 and this page), not stated in the book.

questions.question: What fraction of the data available in the Kaggle competition did the fine-tuned model use for training?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 50%
All of it
questions.answer: About 10%
questions.explanation: The book says 2,000 samples versus 20,000, about 10%. The other options don't match those figures.

questions.question: Can you list the chapter's three strategies for small-data image classification and the test accuracy each reached?
questions.answer: From scratch (78.6%, about 84% with augmentation), feature extraction with a pretrained model (~98%, 98.4% with augmentation), fine-tuning (98.6%).
questions.explanation: See pp.266, 276, 288 and this page.

questions.question: According to the summary, what is the main issue when training a ConvNet on a small dataset?
options: Vanishing gradients
Overfitting
Underfitting
Slow inference
questions.answer: Overfitting
questions.explanation: The third bullet says overfitting will be the main issue, fought with data augmentation. The other options are not what the chapter identified as the main problem.

questions.question: How does the summary describe the relationship between feature extraction and fine-tuning?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning is a complement to feature extraction: it adapts some of the previously learned representations to the new problem and pushes performance a bit further.
questions.explanation: Last bullet; p.288 explains that fine-tuning starts from a feature-extraction model with a trained head.

questions.question: How does the idea that ConvNets learn a 'hierarchy of modular patterns' explain why pretrained features transfer to new datasets?
questions.answer: The lower levels of the hierarchy capture generic visual patterns (edges, textures) useful for almost any image task, so a base trained on a large, general dataset provides reusable features; only the top, more specialized levels may need adapting.
questions.explanation: Combines bullet 2 with the partial fine-tuning sidebar (p.289) and the discussion of generic features on p.280.

questions.question: Which phrase does the summary use for the gain from fine-tuning?
options: It doubles accuracy.
It pushes performance a bit further.
It removes the need for data augmentation.
It is required before feature extraction.
questions.answer: It pushes performance a bit further.
questions.explanation: That is the book's wording. Accuracy went from 98.4% to 98.6%, not doubled; augmentation was still used during fine-tuning; and fine-tuning comes after, not before, feature extraction.

questions.question: For each of the five summary bullets, can you name the experiment in the chapter that illustrated it and the accuracy obtained?
questions.answer: From scratch: 78.6% (p.276); hierarchy of patterns: section 8.1; augmentation: about 84% (p.266); feature extraction: about 98% (pp.285-288); fine-tuning: 98.6% (p.290).
